reverse_outline.summary: Page summary: long planning can still fail to align work, growth splits information from decision authority, and three mechanisms produce alignment
Corvane's planning ate nine of thirteen weeks and still left three teams building the same integration
The usual remedies (more communication, less process) miss the real gap: nobody could name which decisions planning consists of, who makes them, or where they are recorded
The part's thesis that alignment comes from three explicit mechanisms; roadmap of this page and the three chapters

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Asking for Alignment Does Not Produce It ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Growth separates the information a decision needs from the right to make it, leaving three gaps: an informed decider, consistency across teams, and a path for information

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Asking for Alignment Does Not Produce It ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Culture and informal communication only cover people who already talk, so the three gaps must be designed, not left to goodwill
Definitions of the three mechanisms: decision rights and records, planning as three ordered decisions sealed by team objectives, and an operating cadence of forums and documents

Why the mechanisms come in this order (each depends on the previous); how each is judged under the book's two lenses, system design and product thinking, with the planning chapter joining Parts III and IV
The three chapters and the single question each one answers
What reading the chapters in order gives a leader (diagnose a missing mechanism before calling for communication, with Corvane recalled); how to read the part and hand-off to the first chapter

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All nine unit summaries state the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph (p01 to p09); the KEY POINTS callout is page format and matches no spec paragraph.
Introduction ¶3 (two_ideas): the part's claim and the three chapter questions in order are both in p03's controlling idea; the page roadmap is the spec's declared roadmap placement.

Three Mechanisms of Alignment ¶2 (two_ideas): the prerequisite order, the two lenses and the meeting of Parts III and IV are all in p07's controlling idea as the spec states it; the unit holds nothing beyond it. (That the three run together without signals is recorded under flow_is_followable as a minor point.)
Chapters in this part ¶2 (two_ideas): the synthesis, the Corvane callback, the leader's so-what and the hand-off are p09's controlling idea; the reading advice is the conclusion's declared takeaway.

p01 to p03 set up and state the claim; p04 and p05 give the reasoning from which P6-1 to P6-3 are derived; p06 gives one list item per supporting claim; p07 orders them; p08 and p09 map them to chapters. No orphan unit.

Each evidence item is used and interpreted: the Corvane scenario (¶1) is read in ¶2 ('more of it was not what Corvane lacked'); the growth reasoning (p04) and the informal-paths reasoning (p05) end on what they show; the dependency reasoning (p07) is stated with its reasons. Both lists have a lead-in and are followed by a paragraph that interprets them. Note: p06's source item names two books; the draft names Larson only and never names Build What Matters (Foster and Nerlikar), which is not an unexplained piece of evidence but bears on the Larson attribution recorded under flow_is_followable.

results.draft_locus: Three Mechanisms of Alignment ¶1 (Planning bullet) against Introduction ¶3
results.quote: It is three decisions, made in order and separately; the first two are Will Larson's, from *The Engineering Executive's Primer*.
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (a): the lead (and the KEY POINTS and excerpt) prepare two planning steps ('allocating capacity and choosing outcomes are separate steps'), and the bullet gives three decisions, the financial plan appearing here for the first time. A went back to the opening to check the count and assumed the financial plan is a left-out precondition; B had to match the two to the second and third. The section order is not at issue (both readers say so); the bullet needs a clause tying its three decisions to the two steps the lead named. The spec's thesis statement (two steps) and p06 (three decisions) carry the same difference, but prose can bridge it without changing either.

results.quote: You have probably sat through planning like this, which consumes much of the time it plans.
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (b) (A item 1, B item 1): 'the time it plans' needed a second reading before it was taken as 'the quarter it is planning for'. Minor; not blocking.

results.quote: Both skip a question. **Which decisions is planning made of?**
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (b) (A item 2, B item 2): the question arrives abruptly and the next two sentences go back to refuting the two usual answers; only the paragraph's last sentence returns to the question. A suggests placing the two refutations before the question. Minor; not blocking.

results.quote: a decision right for decisions, the cadence for information, and the plan for work, because it says which team's capacity goes to which outcome
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (b) (A item 6, B item 7): the mechanisms are listed here as decision right, cadence, plan, against decision right, plan, cadence everywhere else on the page, and the plan, introduced as what makes many teams' decisions consistent, here serves the flow of work; the 'because' clause resolved the second point. Minor; not blocking.

results.quote: The middle chapter is also where two earlier parts meet.
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (b) (A item 7, B item 9): after the lenses, which concern all three mechanisms, a remark about one chapter felt out of place; both had to work out that 'the middle chapter' is planning, and both would move it next to the Planning bullet. The placement inside p07 is the spec's (its controlling idea includes it), but naming 'the planning chapter' is a wording fix. Minor; not blocking.

results.quote: Each mechanism is also designed and judged under the two lenses through which this book looks at organizations, system design and product thinking.
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (b) (A item 8, B item 8): the paragraph carries three subjects (the dependency order, the two lenses, the meeting of Parts III and IV) with no signal at the joins; A lost track of what the paragraph was for by the middle, B had to slow down at this sentence to see that the dependency argument had ended. Neither left the paragraph. All three subjects are in p07's controlling idea and the one-paragraph form is a recorded spec decision; clearer signals at the two joins are a draft matter. Minor; not blocking.

results.draft_locus: Why Asking for Alignment Does Not Produce It ¶1
results.quote: The second is consistency between the decisions of many teams, since each team decides from its own part.
results.finding: Flow reader B only, item 3, rated (a): the sentence before says 'the right to decide moves up or is never stated', and here the teams are deciding; the reader assumed some decisions stay with teams or that teams decide where nothing is stated. Not reported by reader A. Minor; not blocking.

results.draft_locus: Chapters in this part ¶2 against Why Asking for Alignment Does Not Produce It ¶2
results.quote: At Corvane nobody had said which decisions the nine weeks were for, so the planning could run long and still leave three teams on the same integration.
results.finding: Flow reader B only, item 4, rated (a): the page gives two accounts of the duplicated integration, the unnamed decisions (lead and closing) and the missing path between teams with no reason to meet (first section), and never says which caused it or which mechanism would have caught it; the reader assumed both contribute. Not reported by reader A. The spec's non-goals keep the part's verdict on the nine weeks for chapter 24. Minor; not blocking.

Every does_not_know term is given where it is first used in earnest: alignment ('by which this book means that the work of many teams adds up'), decision right and decision record, financial plan, allocation, capacity, choice of outcomes and team objectives, forums, written artefacts and operating cadence (the list); the lead says 'Each of these terms is defined below' and flow reader A confirms the promise is kept. References to Parts I, III and IV are within already_knows. Neither flow reader reported a term as unexplained.
Opens on a concrete scenario with numbers and a question; no placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book-report opening.
The closing does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic and does not end on a rephrased thesis alone: it gives a synthesis, the callback, the so-what, reading advice and the hand-off.

Synthesis ('the three chapters follow a decision from who makes it, through the plan that many such decisions add up to, to the rhythm of meetings and documents') is stated by no single section; so-what ('a leader who finds teams pulling apart looks for the missing decision right, the planning steps tangled into one or the absent forum before calling for better communication') is present, with the takeaway and the hand-off.

'At Corvane nobody had said which decisions the nine weeks were for, so the planning could run long and still leave three teams on the same integration' reads the opening scenario against the lead's question, as the spec's callback states.

The cold intro reader predicted both roadmap promises in order: why alignment does not arise by itself as an organization grows (growth separating information from the right to decide, goodwill not repairing it), then the three mechanisms each defined, closing on three chapters answering the three questions.
The cold reader named the three subjects in reading order: decision rights and decision records; planning; operating cadence, matching the expected answer, and called the page very clear on this.
